title: What I received (1 Corinthians 11:23–26)
hook: the earliest written account of the Last Supper

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul told the Corinthians that the body is a temple of the Holy Ghost, bought at a price. Your line was bought with a price. Did you give your body a little rest? Day five hundred seventy-two.

Most scholars think that before Matthew, Mark, Luke or John had set down a single line, a letter crossed the sea from Ephesus to Corinth. Paul had heard something that made him angry. The Christians of Corinth met for the Lord's Supper in a member's house, and it had turned into a dinner party with a cruel side. The well-off ate their fill, and some even got drunk. The poor, perhaps arriving late from work, found nothing left. To correct them, Paul does something nobody had done in writing yet, as far as we know. He sets down the words of the Last Supper.
screen: `A LETTER BEFORE THE GOSPELS.` → `A SUPPER GONE WRONG IN CORINTH.` → `PAUL WRITES DOWN THE LAST SUPPER.`

segments.voice: He opens with a formula, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." Received, delivered. In Greek these are the words teachers used for handing on a tradition, the way a student passes on exactly what a teacher said. Paul isn't inventing anything. He's passing along a chain that was already in place, roughly twenty years after the cross. Then come the words themselves. The Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said: "Take ye, and eat: this is my body, which shall be delivered for you: this do for the commemoration of me." Then the cup: the new testament in his blood. In the Greek, one verb is doing double work here. Paul handed on the tradition, and that night Jesus was handed over. Then Paul adds his own line: "For as often as you shall eat this bread, and drink the chalice, you shall shew the death of the Lord, until he come." Every celebration of the supper, he's saying, announces something. That's why the Corinthians' carelessness shocks him. A few verses later he warns that whoever eats and drinks unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Catholics read this page as a witness to what happens at every Mass. The priest's words at the consecration come from these accounts, in Paul and in the Gospels, and the Church teaches that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Other Christians understand the supper in other ways, as a spiritual presence or as a memorial, and they reach for this same page. It's very likely the oldest written account we have of words still said at altars every day.
screen: `RECEIVED AND DELIVERED: A TRADITION.` · `THIS IS MY BODY, DELIVERED FOR YOU.` · `YOU SHOW THE LORD'S DEATH.` · `WORDS STILL SAID AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THIS DO FOR THE COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry Paul's words to the next consecration. If you'll be at Mass this week, wait for the moment the priest lifts the host and then the chalice. Many Catholics silently say Thomas's words then: my Lord and my God. For now, wherever you are, settle and breathe. Picture a table in a house in Corinth, bread broken, a cup passed from hand to hand. Then think of who handed on to you whatever you hold most dear: a faith, a recipe, a way of praying. If you pray, you can say today's line slowly. If you don't, simply remember them with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Commemoration. Jesus's words over the bread at the Last Supper, do this for the commemoration of me, handed down to Paul and on to Corinth. Today's word.
Your line: I received of the lord. Today, notice one thing someone handed on to you, a habit, a prayer, a story, and pass it on to one person. Day five hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: At every Mass the priest says the words of institution over the bread and the chalice; Catholics kneel, the host and chalice are raised, and in many parishes a bell is rung.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you hear that at Corinth's Lord's Supper the rich eat first and the poor go hungry. what do you write?
options: let each house meet however suits it.
cancel the supper until they behave.
write out the words of the Last Supper and remind them what it is.
fork.reveal: he writes down what he received: "this is my body, which shall be delivered for you." the meal they were treating as a party, he says, shows the Lord's death.

original.note: Greek: I received. the word for taking over a tradition that is handed down (1 Corinthians 11:23).

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul retelling a Gospel scene.
what it means: Paul hands on words he received, written before any Gospel, to correct a supper that shamed the poor.
what a scholar hears: paralambanō and paradidōmi, the technical pair for passing on tradition; paradidōmi also names the night Jesus was handed over.

notes: Dating: 1 Corinthians is usually dated about AD 53–55, before the written Gospels; 'about twenty years after the cross' is approximate. Confirm.
Check the exact Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of 1 Corinthians 11:23, 11:24 and 11:26.
paralambanō/paradidōmi as technical terms for handing on tradition (compare 1 Corinthians 15:3); paradidōmi also in 'the night in which he was betrayed'. Confirm.
Custom of silently saying 'My Lord and my God' at the elevation: a widespread devotion, not a rubric. Confirm phrasing.

Review edit: hook softened to 'most scholars think' (Gospel dating vs. 1 Corinthians is the majority view, not settled); 'the poor came late from work' is a scholarly reconstruction (e.g. Theissen) from 11:21, 33, now hedged with 'perhaps'; 'oldest written copy' changed to 'very likely the oldest written account' (no autograph or earliest copy is implied).
Practice reworded from the outline ('pray at the next consecration with Paul') to work for listeners not at Mass.
